scenes.headline: pandas: GroupBy, Merge & Join
scenes.subtitle: Aggregating and combining datasets
scenes.narration: Aggregation and joins are the heart of analytics in pandas, mirroring the GROUP BY and JOIN operations you already know from SQL.

scenes.headline: Split-Apply-Combine
scenes.narration: GroupBy is best understood as split-apply-combine. pandas first partitions the rows into groups by one or more keys, then applies an aggregation function within each group, and finally combines those per-group results back into a single tidy structure. Every aggregation you write follows this pattern under the hood.

scenes.headline: GroupBy aggregation
scenes.narration: The first line groups rows by country and sums spend within each group, producing one total per country. The second uses agg with named outputs to compute several metrics in a single pass, here both a spend total and a distinct user count. Named aggregation keeps result columns readable and lets you build a full summary table at once.

scenes.headline: merge vs concat
scenes.narration: Use merge when you need to combine two frames by matching values in a key column, exactly like a SQL join that aligns related records. Use concat when you simply want to stack frames together, whether appending rows from another period or gluing columns side by side, with no key matching involved. Choosing the right one prevents both wrong results and needless complexity.

scenes.headline: Joining DataFrames
scenes.code:
orders.merge(
    customers,
    on='customer_id',
    how='left',      # inner, left, right, outer
)
scenes.narration: This merges orders with customers on their shared customer_id. The how argument controls the join type just as in SQL: a left join keeps every order and attaches matching customer details, filling gaps with nulls where no match exists. Switching how to inner, right, or outer changes exactly which rows survive.

scenes.headline: Join gotchas
items: Check row counts before and after
scenes.narration: Duplicate keys on both sides multiply rows together, quietly exploding your result far beyond what you intended. A key that is an integer on one side and a string on the other simply fails to match, dropping records. Passing validate tells pandas to assert the cardinality you expect and error if it's violated. And comparing row counts before and after every merge is the simplest safeguard against silent data corruption.

scenes.text: Pick how= deliberately, watch for duplicate keys, and verify row counts after every merge.
scenes.narration: Choose your join type deliberately and check row counts after every merge, and you'll catch the duplicate-key blowups that silently wreck analytics.
